newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Navigating auctions, budget.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Navigating auctions, budget.

text.p: U.S. fixed income markets should be dominated by technical trade next week and dealers will tread gingerly around the quarterly Treasury refunding and the details of the Washington budget deal announced Friday, market experts said.

"I'm a little worried the market might not like the details (of the budget pact). So you might have an adverse reaction on that," said Carey Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
The schedule of big events in the coming days is light and analysts said Treasuries may have a touch of technical heartburn after a blizzard of economic data fueled a sharp rally this week.
"There will be a lot of technical type of adjustment," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston. "The budget stuff could be interesting."

Technically, U.S. Treasury securities may need to digest this week's solid gains, which pushed the yield on the benchmark 30-year bond below the key 7.0 percent level for the first time in more than a month, the experts said.

The long-bond is hesitating on the cusp of concluding the downtrend in place from February, when the bond yielded about 6.50 percent, to mid-April when it closed at a cycle-high yield of 7.17 percent, analysts said.

The bond yield tapped a low of 6.88 percent on Friday. But it could not extend its gains in late Friday trade even after a Clinton administration official said the White House and Congressional Republicans had reached a deal to balance the governmennt's budget by 2002.

A yield below 6.88 percent would be bullish for the bond. But in the short end of the maturity curve, the two-year note has to rally past a yield of 6.19 percent, from its current 6.24 percent, for acceleration, Alexy said.
Some analysts said they were concerned the rally might falter next week.
"The chart patterns look good but now we're not behaving very well," said Chris Rupkey, financial economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
"If we go above 7.0 percent during next week's auctions its going to be bad," he added.
At 1600 EDT on Friday, the T-bond was trading up 9/32 at 96.21/32, with a yield of 6.90 percent.
The Treasury kicks off its quarterly refunding with the auction of $17 billion in three-year notes Tuesday and concludes Wednesday with $12 billion in 10-year notes.
With no 30-year paper to absorb, the market should have little serious difficulty digesting new supply, economists said.
The credit markets are unlikely to pay much attention to March factory orders, due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT Tuesday, but could get a boost from data the next day, experts said.
Factory orders are expected to have fallen 1.5 percent in March after a gain of 0.8 percent in February.
"We never really move on that thing. Realistically we already have durable goods," Rupkey said.
On Wednesday, the Federal Reserve's survey of regional economic activity -- known as the Beige Book -- will be scrutinized for signs of broad-based growth.
Also on Wednesday comes first-quarter labor productivity data.

"With the strong first-quarter growth rate of the economy, you're probably going to be looking at a labor productivity growth rate in excess of two percent. You would be talking about trend unit labor costs, which are moving down compared to last year's 2.7 percent pace. So I think that's going to be favorable," Leahey said.
